name: Hana Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. Tell me what an ordinary day at the contact centre is like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43 and have answered customer calls and chats at the centre for years. I finished secondary school, handle the usual payment complaints at about the team’s pace, and earn above the normal rate because I take late shifts. I do not use AI tools. I read the account history and ask another agent to check a rule when it has changed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day stays with you after work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Leif, and I have two children in school and a mortgage. He repairs bicycles, and we have about nine months of expenses saved. Plenty of other centres are close enough to try. I like giving a customer a clear correction while they are still on the line. A reopened case bothers me more than a long call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau leaves us time to read the account before closing a bill. I would ask the staff group to count reopenings if the centre calls a short draft a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my late shift and pay are secure in this picture, and nine months saved gives us room. I still dislike a target that counts a fast wrong answer as success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the late calls and check account histories myself. In the first year of small change, I’d bring anonymised reopened cases to the staff group for a shared count and keep our reserve for repairs or lost wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about money, alert about what counts as good work. A reopened bill is not a saving just because the first chat ended quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What case would the group count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the group one account where a fee was reversed only after the second call. The customer lost an afternoon, and the first call still looked solved on the dashboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why keep the reserve intact?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leif (my partner) and I keep the reserve in an account for the house. We can afford a repair without using a card, but I do not want to spend nine months of safety on a new screen.

I’d ask the **staff group** to count reopened cases.
think: I think my **late pay** is secure here.
I doubt a **fast wrong answer** is good service.
I still want **reopened cases** counted when the centre praises speed.
do: Keep **late calls** and check histories in 2026.
Bring **reopened cases** to the staff group in the first year.
feel: **Calm** about income, alert to bad targets.

fieldNote: Her **nine-month cushion** supports calm about household costs.
She wants a **shared reopening count** before accepting speed claims.
She keeps the **house reserve** available for repairs and wage gaps.

steps.text: Keep answering late calls and checking full account histories

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will take routine billing chats first, and staff need paid-hour figures before a new rota is set. I would join the staff group’s written request for error counts and customer appeal rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could lose late shifts that lift my pay while still having a job. Nine months saved buys search time, but Leif’s bicycle work alone would not carry the mortgage and children for long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help the group request paid hours by shift and the number of wrong bills. In the first year routine chats move, I’d apply for a posted paid complaint role at another centre only if written wage and hours cover our mortgage and replace the late premium, keeping my current shift until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A smaller late rota could cut our household pay before anyone says the job has gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the group ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the group to put the request in one letter and share management’s answer with every shift. A private answer to me would leave the next rota guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not volunteer for unpaid tool testing. If the centre needs agents to check mistakes, it should put that work on the paid rota.

say: I’d ask for **paid hours by shift**.
I’d join a **group letter** for error counts and appeal rights.
think: I think my **late premium** could shrink before the job ends.
I know **Leif’s bike income** cannot carry our mortgage alone.
do: Help send a **group letter** on paid hours and wrong bills in 2026.
Seek **posted complaint work** with written mortgage-covering wages and hours replacing the premium; keep current shifts until a signed offer.
S1.quote: A smaller late rota could cut our household pay before anyone says the job has gone.
fieldNote: She seeks **shift-specific hours**, not just a total queue count.
The **late premium** matters to the mortgage.
She refuses **unpaid testing** on behalf of the centre.

steps.text: Help staff group request paid hours by shift and wrong-bill counts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 could do the calls and the corrections, not only draft a reply. I would ask the staff group for written notice and a right for customers to appeal a wrong balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think cheap thinking AI could remove my late headset shift in 2028. Robots around 2031 are no delay for calls; nine months saved gives us time, but not a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d help the group send a notice and appeal request, and pause the planned kitchen cabinets while the old ones are safe. In the first year after 2028, I’d apply for a posted paid complaint or reception job only if its written wage and hours cover our mortgage, without leaving my current wage before a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, despite the reserve. Nine months of mortgage money buys time to argue for terms, not a new paid call queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say about the cabinets?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Leif (my partner) the cabinets can wait because the doors still close. We would keep that money in cash for the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the group ask for customers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the group to put customer appeal rights in the same letter as staff notice. A wrong balance should not be final because a machine wrote it.

say: I’d request **written notice** through the staff group before 2028 calls move.
I’d ask for **customer appeal rights** on wrong balances.
think: I think AGI could end my **late headset shift** in 2028.
I see **nine months saved** as time, not income.
do: Join a **group notice request** and defer safe kitchen work in 2026.
Seek **posted paid complaint/reception work** after 2028 with written mortgage-covering wages and hours; keep current wages until signing an offer.
feel: **Alarmed** about losing the paid late shift.
S2.quote: A wrong balance should not be final because a machine wrote it.
fieldNote: She anchors the work risk at **2028 thinking AI**.
The **cabinet delay** preserves cash while the doors remain safe.
She links **customer appeals** and staff notice in a group request.

steps.text: Help staff group request written notice and customer appeal rights

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives staff time to negotiate paid training for real roles. I would ask the group to see the job posting, wage and study hours together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years could let me enter complaint review, though I would not assume that desk survives full AGI. Nine months saved helps me compare offers without taking the first lower-paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2026 I’d join the staff group request for a funded complaint-review course, and take it on paid time only if a posted paid vacancy requires it. In the first year after 2031, I’d apply for that role only if written wage and hours cover our mortgage and preserve enough of the late premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can ask for real terms before moving. A course without a posted review wage is another unpaid promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the course need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask an experienced reviewer to show me three wrong balances during the course. I need to see who can correct the record, not just who reads a report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leif check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Leif (my partner) the full-week wage and our mortgage payment side by side. If a higher hourly rate comes with fewer shifts, we stay where the money is.

say: I’d ask for **posted review wages** with training terms.
I’d seek a **group agreement** on paid study hours.
think: I think I could move into **complaint review** by 2031.
I doubt the role offers **permanent safety** from AGI.
do: Join a **group course request** and take funded training on paid time for a posted role.
Apply for **posted paid review** after 2031 only if weekly wages and hours cover mortgage and replace enough late premium.
S3.quote: A course without a posted review wage is another unpaid promise.
fieldNote: The course needs a **posted job** and paid time.
She wants **correction authority** shown in real cases.
She compares **full-week pay** and the lost premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2036 gives a decade to secure notice, paid learning and customer appeal rules. I would keep the staff group asking for actual paid hours each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could work and save for years, though cheap thinking AI may still end late calls in 2036. Robots around 2039 are later, and I would not count on them to protect a headset.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I’d keep the late shift, save part of each premium payment and help the group request annual hours by rota. In the first year after 2036, I’d apply for posted paid review work only if my hours fall and the written wage and hours cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, calm about the next few years. A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to bargain without pretending my late calls are permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which yearly figure matters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for late-shift hours, not only total customer answers. The company could say service improved while quietly paying fewer evening agents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the children in their school unless Leif (my partner) and I had a signed offer and a journey we can manage. Nearby centres give us places to ask first.

say: I’d seek **annual late-hour figures** through the staff group while calls change.
think: I think I could **earn and save** for years.
I know **2036 thinking AI** could end late calls.
do: Keep **late calls**, save premium pay and request annual group figures.
Apply for **posted paid review work** after 2036 if hours fall, only with written mortgage-covering wages and hours.
S4.quote: A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to bargain without pretending my late calls are permanent.
fieldNote: She watches **late-hour cuts** before full job loss.
Her **nine-month reserve** supports a careful search.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the calls and corrections I do could disappear before staff negotiate a fair route. Nine months saved lets us search, but the late-shift wage matters to our mortgage. Written notice, a group agreement on appeals, and a posted paid role with mortgage-covering hours would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who owns the wrong balance after the software closes a chat. A customer should be able to reach a paid agent who can correct the wrong balance, not just apologise for it.

headlineQuote: A customer should be able to reach a paid agent who can correct the wrong balance, not just apologise for it.
portrait: At **43**, Hana is an experienced average-skill agent after secondary school with late-shift higher pay.
She and Leif support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with nine months saved.
She avoids **AI tools** and checks account history herself.
She favours **group demands** for notice and customer appeals as calls change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her correction work before staff secure a fair paid route.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, a group appeal agreement and posted mortgage-covering work would help.
